draft.title: Compound interest
card: With compound interest, the interest earned is added to the balance. The next period's interest is then worked out on the larger amount. So interest earns interest.
The formula is \(A = P(1 + r)^{n}\). \(A\) is the final amount, \(P\) is the amount invested at the start, \(r\) is the rate per period as a decimal, and \(n\) is the number of periods.

Compare with simple interest, which is always worked out on the starting amount. On $2000 at 5% a year for 3 years, simple interest gives $2300. Compound interest gives $2315.25, because the interest also earns interest.
Example: $2000 at 5% per year for 3 years. \(A = 2000 \times 1.05^{3} = 2000 \times 1.157625 = \$2315.25\). The interest earned is $315.25.
draft.remember: Multiply by \((1 + r)\) once for each period. Match \(r\) and \(n\) to the same period.

a.q: Mia puts $1000 in an account paying 10% per year, compounded yearly. How much is in the account after 2 years?
a.why: \(A = 1000 \times 1.1^{2} = 1000 \times 1.21 = \$1210\). The answer $1200 is simple interest, which does not let the interest earn interest.
a.clue: Is the second year's interest found on $1000 or on the new balance?

b.q: Sam puts $5000 in an account paying 6% per year, compounded monthly. Which calculation gives the balance after 2 years?
b.why: The rate per month is \(0.06 \div 12 = 0.005\), and there are \(2 \times 12 = 24\) months. So \(A = 5000 \times 1.005^{24}\). Using \(1.06^{2}\) ignores the monthly compounding, so the rate and periods do not match.
b.clue: Convert both the rate and the time to months.
